item.title: ALDS Game 2 Player of the Game: Ben Rice
item.author: Jeremy Nielsen
item.content:encoded: The Yankees have lost an ugly game in the ALDS yet again. As a result of another contest in which they were played off the field by a division rival, they are once again compelled to win three straight games facing elimination to keep their season alive. The Yankees have never won a postseason series under Aaron Boone as the underdog—and through two games their lifeless, gormless play has proven immune to the best-laid pitching plans of one of the most dominant pitching staffs in franchise history.If you’re looking for a hero in this 5-2 loss at Tropicana Field, you’re going to have to keep looking. At least unlike Saturday there was a number above zero on New York’s side of the scorecard. Ben Rice provided those two tallies with a pair of home runs to right, the first of which provided a brief spark of hope that the Yankees might not totally butcher this thing—before they totally butchered it just two innings later.Rice hit a flyout in his first at-bat, precipitating a perfect first time through the order for Rays starter Freddy Peralta. But his second time up promised a better future for this game and this series. Fastball Freddy, as the broadcast referred to him roughly a dozen times throughout the night, started Rice off with said fastball before abandoning it in favor of his changeup. He made three successive attempts to lure Rice into chasing the pitch—and his third try was successful to bring the count to 2-2.That whiff seemed to further convince Peralta to stick with his change, especially knowing that Rice is one of the league’s best fastball hitters. So for the fourth straight time, he went changeup away—but he left this one in the strike zone, along the outside corner. Rice capitalized, shooting it over the right field wall for a game-tying solo blast.Rice did his job effectively again when he came up for a third time in the fifth inning. With two outs, Austin Wells doubled off Peralta to spark a rally. Ryan McMahon followed by working a walk after falling behind 0-2, which ended Peralta’s night. Rice was the first man to face lefty reliever Cam Booser, and got nothing good to swing at. The southpaw pitched around Ben, who refused to expand the zone. He worked his walk to load the bases for Cody Bellinger, known for his track record of success against left-handed pitching. Bellinger very nearly found the go-ahead hit he was looking for with a long fly ball to center field, but Jonny DeLuca ran it down on the warning track.Of course, the Rays benefitted from a Yankee pratfall routine immediately afterward, destroying all positive momentum and building a 5-1 lead. But Rice, outcome be damned, was gonna turn in another good at-bat. Facing Ian Seymour to lead off the eighth inning, he took a first-pitch sweeper for a strike, then unleashed a lightning-fast swing on an inside changeup. His line drive down the right field line snuck over the wall for his second homer of the night.Rice could not spark a greater rally. The Yankees went down in order against Seymour right after that second homer, and put up no resistance against closer Bryan Baker. The Yankees are on the verge on another ignominious end to a strong season, but at the very least we can give a tip of the hat to their best hitter all year, who never gave in even as the rest of the team kept making the same familiar mistakes that routinely send this team home emptyhanded in October.If a miraculous and frankly uncharacteristic series victory from down 2-0 is in the offing, no doubt Ben Rice will be one of the key reasons. The Yankees will need more than just him to hit, but his exceptional talent must also continue to be front-and-center for the Bombers to save their season.

item.title: We rate the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 as some of our best headphones for cyclists, and they're now less than half price during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days
item.author: Rich Owen
item.content:encoded: We ranked the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 as best for Android users in our recently updated best headphones for cycling buying guide. Right now, you can save up to 55% when you buy them at Amazon UK as part of its Big Deal Days sale.There is a small catch, as only the pink-tipped earbuds are available at this price. I think they look very cool, but if they don't work for you, the black and grey-tipped options still have a decent £60 saving. Another money-saving option for those not swayed by the pink would be to buy official replacement tips for £19, or unofficial ones for £8.The UK deal is not exclusive to Prime Members, but should you want to sign up, you can geta and cancel anytime before the £8.99 ($14.99 US) monthly fee kicks in.Tester Will Jones gave the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 4.5 out of 5 stars in our best headphones for cycling guide, ranking them as best for Android. They have a best-in-class battery life of 12 hours and are comfortable when worn for long periods, making them ideal for all-day rides.View DealIf you're in the US, the Pixel Buds Pro 2s are part of Amazon's Big Deal Days sale too, with a 22% saving, which drops the price to $179. There's no colour conundrum here though, as every hue is the same price.As well as being super comfortable and being able to go 12 hours between charges, the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 have excellent gesture controls. There's also an iOS-like 'Find My' feature – which is invaluable if you can't remember which jacket pocket you last stuck them in, or if they should slip down the back of the couch.Noise cancellation is decent, and there's transparency mode and conversation detection too. The Pro 2s are designed to cope with wet weather and come with an IP54 rating. The gesture controls can go haywire in the wet though, so Will suggests turning that function off when riding in the rain.Overall audio performance is very good, but it's not quite up to the likes of Technics EAH-AZ100.If you're in the market for these excellent earbuds, don't hang about as Amazon Big Deal Days ends at midnight Wednesday, 7 October.Other Amazon Big Deal Days 2026 deals

item.title: Canyon-SRAM strengthen sprint and Classics lineup with Georgia Baker signing
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Canyon-SRAM have announced the signing of former track world champion Georgia Baker from Liv-AlUla-Jayco, the team's third addition for 2027.Baker joins Swiss duo Jasmin Liechti and Steffi Häberlin on the incoming list for the German team as Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Maike van der Duin, and the retiring Tiffany Cromwell depart.32-year-old Baker has experienced success on the track and road during a top-level career which stretches back more than a decade. In 2019, she was part of Australia's World Championship-winning team pursuit lineup, and she's also won two Commonwealth Games golds on the track."Georgia brings a very valuable combination of speed, power, versatility and tactical know-how. She has the physical qualities of a sprinter but is also capable of performing in the harder and more technical races," said Canyon-SRAM performance director Dan Fleeman.He explained that Baker can work in a sprint lead-out train as well as excel in the Classics, where she's collected top-five finishes at Scheldeprijs, the Classic Brugge-De Panne, and Le Samyn over the years."She can play an important role in lead-out and positioning work during the final kilometres, putting sprinters in the best possible position, while in the classics, she has the ability to not just survive, but also contribute when the going gets tough."Georgia’s versatility is very valuable because it gives us different options depending on how a race develops, and there’s also the potential for her to take her own opportunities when the situation allows."Baker said that she's excited to take on a new challenge, having spent the last five years at Liv."I think I’m most excited by the opportunity for a fresh start and a new challenge. Canyon-SRAM is a team that I’ve always respected from the outside, and I’m really looking forward to learning from a new group of people and hopefully bringing my own experience to the team as well," she said."I still love racing my bike, and I still feel like there’s more that I want to achieve. As I’ve gotten older, I think that my motivation has actually evolved. Of course, I still want to win and get the best out of myself, but I also really enjoy being part of a team, helping other riders succeed, and continuing to challenge myself in different ways."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: UEC defends accuracy of photo finish at European Championships in response to Giulio Ciccone questioning technology
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: The Italian pleaded to see more proof that he had fallen just millimetres short of the victory on Sunday, having led out the two-up sprint in Slovenia and only been caught on the line by Evenepoel's last-ditch bike throw. His disappointment in Šenčur turned to bewilderment 24 hours later, and he said that "in the filming where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing a dynamic that I cannot reconcile with that verdict."In the two photo finishes that were released by the organisers, questions were raised due to the distortion of Ciccone's bike size, and the minuscule gap which had Evenepoel pipping him to the line. In information provided to EvoData, the company that did the timing for the Europeans, explained that the time difference was just 0.0002 seconds (0.2 milliseconds), an estimated gap of 2.8 to 3.3 millimetres when translated onto the road.The UEC explained how the finish line technology works in a press release, stressing that neither a normal camera is used nor a normal photograph is produced at the line, and detailed why the visible distortions have no effect on the accuracy of the result given."The Union Européenne de Cyclisme (UEC) states that the photo-finish system used at the 2026 UEC Road European Championships (EtherLynx Vision PRO X) records the finish line thousands of times per second (13,000 in the specific case of the European Championship races), making it possible to determine the order of arrival with extreme precision, even in the event of minimal differences," read the press release."It is important to clarify that the photo-finish is not a traditional photograph. The final image is composed of the chronological sequence of recordings taken at the finish line. For this reason, the horizontal axis represents time and not distance."This can create apparent distortions of wheels, bicycles and riders, without affecting the accuracy of the result in any way."Several social media users have tried to buy into Ciccone's theory by examining traditional photos of the finish line, but the gap from the line on the road and the part of the rider's front wheel which crosses the line first is too far apart to accurately determine who arrived first.Again defending their thorough process, which positions photo finish cameras at either side of the line to verify their accuracy, the UEC looked to move on from the controversy as the Championships continue in Slovenia this week with the time trials. "In cycling, the decisive reference point is the foremost part (tangent) of the front wheel at the exact moment it crosses the finish line," read the statement."At the European Championships, two independent photo-finish systems are used, which provide two separate images for verification of the result."The UEC will not issue any further statements on this matter."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: ‘They take our water, our soil’: protesters fight ‘foreignisation’ as Javier Milei encourages land sales in Argentina
item.author: Valentina Di Liscia. Photographs by Roxana Sposaro
item.content:encoded: The country’s far-right president is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resourcesOn 19 September, Marta Sahores, an 84-year-old chemistry professor and activist who has mobilised against mega-mining projects for more than two decades, took to the streets in Argentina. Alongside workers, retirees, students, Indigenous groups and human rights organisations, Sahores was there to protest against the country’s far-right president, Javier Milei. During the – the “march of anger” – protesters held signs reading, among other rallying cries, “The land is not for sale”.Marching in Esquel, a town nestled in the foothills of the Andes in Chubut province, she also held up a sign defending the country’s water resources against what she called the government’s “handover” to investors.Continue reading...

item.title: An open field with no Evenepoel or Ganna – Analysing the European Championships elite men's time trial contenders
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Remco Evenepoel may have won the rainbow stripes in Canada to crown himself once again as the world's greatest time trialist, but the Belgian won't be present in Šenčur to go for the European title a third time.Italian racer Filippo Ganna, who was top dog before Evenepoel came along, won't be present either, while the new cannibal Tadej Pogačar is also out. There's a wide-open field at the elite men's time trial at this year's UEC Road European Championships, then.44 riders will tackle the 22.1km route in Šenčur, a challenging ride which features a two-in-one climb (2km at 10% and 900 metres at 4.7%) in the middle of the course – a feature which will have an outsized impact on the final result.Last year's podium sitters Evenepoel, Ganna, and Dane Niklas Larsen aren't racing in Slovenia, so there'll be a trio of new faces atop the podium. There may very well be a first-time champion, too, with double champion Stefan Küng the only rider present to have won this title before.So who's in the frame for the 2026 European title? Read on to find out.With the biggest names on the time trial scene not taking part in Tuesday's race, Swiss specialist Stefan Küng looks likely to step into the role of the top favourite for the blue bands of European champion.He has won the event twice before, in 2020 and 2021, and he has finished on the podium another two times, taking a heartbreaking second place by a single second behind countryman Stefan Bissegger in Fürstenfeldbruck in 2022 and missing out to Edoardo Affini by nine seconds in Hasselt two years later.The 32-year-old has been in good form recently, having scored his second career Vuelta a España stage victory last month with a two-second victory over Callum Thornley in Jerez de la Frontera on stage 18.He wasn't on the podium at the Road World Championships, though, finishing in seventh place in the time trial, 1:44 down on world champion Evenepoel, and he also finished 18 seconds behind fellow competitor here, Jakob Söderqvist.With no Tadej Pogačar in the lineup, Primož Roglič heads into the race as Slovenia's great hope of a result.The veteran racer has only taken part in one European Championships time trial in his career, finishing 16th at the 2016 Euros. He has fared better at the Worlds, meanwhile, scoring a silver medal the next year behind Tom Dumoulin.36-year-old Roglič has certainly enjoyed an uptick in form in recent months, racing to second overall at the Vuelta a España, by far his best result of the season. His time trial effort in Jerez de la Frontera saw him place fourth in the 32.1km test, behind Küng and Thornley. He's certainly among the favourites for a medal on the hilly course in Šenčur.Jakob Söderqvist may only be a neo-pro, but he signed his Lidl-Trek contract as one of the most promising young time trialists in the world. In his final two years before turning pro, the Swede triumphed against the clock at the Worlds under-23 TT, the Flèche du Sud, Giro Next Gen, and under-23 Chrono des Nations, as well as adding Worlds and European silver to his collection.Söderqvist started his year with a third place in the Volta ao Algarve TT before going on to second places in prologues at the Tour de Romandie and Boucles de la Mayenne, winning the Swedish national title, and, most recently, coming away with fifth place in Montreal, 1:26 off Evenepoel.At 23, Söderqvist is one of the youngest men in the race, but he's well in the running for a medal.The first of the two Danish riders on our list, Mikkel Bjerg has twice come close to a medal in the European Championships, finishing 18 seconds adrift of bronze in 2022 and 26 seconds off the following year.Bjerg hasn't been in the best form of his career this season, with eighth place in the 42km time trial to Massa at the Giro d'Italia his best TT result outside of the Danish Championships. Still, this race represents a better chance at a higher ranking for him, given the top contenders who won't be here.As with some others on this list, the course isn't particularly to his advantage given the big hill which should be a deciding factor in the outcome of the medal placings. Still, he's a quality time triallist and should be there or thereabouts.Bruno Armirail is France's main hope, though the 32-year-old is among the outsiders for a medal. His best result to date in three appearances at the Euros is ninth place on home ground last year.He finished 26th at the recent Worlds time trial in Montreal, but impressed in the stage 16 TT at the Tour de France and in the stage 18 TT at the Vuelta, coming away with eighth and seventh places respectively.That does suggest somewhat that his strength has been in recovering for those late-race efforts, something which obviously won't apply here in a one-off event.The second Dane on our list is Kasper Asgreen, who can point to a strong record at this race, having finished in second, seventh, and eighth in three appearances dating back to 2019. His most recent outing came in Hasselt two years ago, where he finished eighth, 1:06 down on the champion Edoardo Affini.Asgreen's form is looking up as he heads to Slovenia, too, with eighth place at the Montreal (where only Söderqvist and Küng from the Euros startlist finished ahead of him) his outstanding result of the past two seasons. He could be in with a shot at a medal here.23-year-old Callum Thornley is another young hopeful on the list aiming for a high placing in Šenčur.The Scottish rider enjoyed a great run of time trial results recently, including third at the Tour de Pologne and fourth and second places at the two Vuelta a España tests, with the second seeing him miss out on the win by just two seconds to Küng.His most recent outing on the time trial bike saw him take 10th place in Montreal, just over two minutes behind world champion Remco Evenepoel and 18 seconds off Küng. Like Söderqvist, Thornley looks destined to be a top time trial contender for years to come – will either of the young hopefuls hit those heights well ahead of schedule here?The Netherlands' best hope lies with , whose standout time trial result this season was third place in that 42km Giro time trial. The one-time Dutch TT champion will be competing at the Euros for the second time after finishing 10th in 2023.With no Filippo Ganna, it's up to to lead Italian hopes. The 35-year-old was recently part of his nation's triumphant ride to mixed relay TTT success at the Worlds, while he finished the individual time trial in 16th place. His ride to sixth place in the hilly late time trial at the Tour de France also stands out in our memory. is Spain's sole entrant in the time trial. The former national champion and under-23 world champion picked up silver here in the under-23 race three years ago, and he's in good form at the moment, having raced to fifth place in the road race.Slovenia's second rider comes in the form of , one of eight riders at this race to have finished in the top 20 at Worlds. He was 17th in Montreal, ahead of Hayter and just behind Romeo and Cattaneo. Tratnik has been up there at the Euros before, finishing sixth at the 2020 time trial.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: Brilliant Rays bats, brutal Yankees defense leave Bombers in 2-0 hole
item.author: Jake Devin
item.content:encoded: It’s rare that a hitter feels in full control of a plate appearance. Hitting is an inherently reactive activity, with the pitcher in control of what pitch is thrown, how it’s thrown, where it’s thrown, even when and why it’s thrown. It’s even more difficult for the hitter to feel in control when facing a dominant pitcher, with elite arms attacking the opposition and making them feel as if they’re on the wrong side of an avalanche. Which makes Monday’s offensive performance from the Rays all that more impressive. Facing the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, Tampa’s hitters were in control all night. They made Cam Schlittler sweat, they made him work, and in the end, they made him bleed. The end result was a 5-2 Rays victory, a commanding 2-0 series lead, and another Yankees season on life support.Schlittler was coming off a stellar performance in a season consisting almost exclusively of stellar performances. He diced up the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, leaning on his curveball in a surprise manuever that left Boston gasping for air. Schlitter’s strategy wasn’t quite as curve heavy this time around, using it 18 percent of the time compared to 27 percent versus Boston, electing to go after Tampa with his trademark high-heat, three-fastball approach.The Rays were ready. Tampa’s hitters have the flattest swings of any team in the league, which in theory should make them a tough matchup for Schlittler, with their swing paths putting the bat right on plane to make contact with Schlittler’s fastballs. In practice, Schlittler proved unable to overpower them. Schlittler managed only seven swings and misses, a total he failed to reach just once during this magnificent season. The Rays struck out twice versus the right-hander, the lowest mark all year for Schlittler. Tampa’s hitters just never seemed uncomfortable facing the best pitcher in the American League. They never expanded the zone, rarely found themselves in unfavorable counts, and made hard contact in nearly every inning against Schlittler. The Rays’ swings always seemed to be on time, fair or foul:And even their takes exuded confidence:It was a remarkable feat, to stare down the most intimidating pitcher in the league and to force him to blink, not vice versa.On a day where his defense or offense backed him up, Schlittler still might have been able to make it work, to grind through five or six innings and eek out a win. Instead, New York played one of its sloppiest games ever, tallying a staggering four (later changed by the official scorer from five) errors in the span of six innings, three in the first frame alone. You can thank the Rays’ fast, aggressive play style in part, forcing the Yankee fielders to speed up:But the Yankees just failed to execute on defense in the most important game of the year, something that has happened before. Ryan McMahon booted the first batted ball of the game, Jazz Chisholm Jr. threw a ball away on an ill-fated attempt to turn two in the first, and in the fifth, George Lombard Jr. a committed a fielding error and also a throwing error that was later changed to a fielder’s choice, helping the Rays along to their four-run outburst that ultimately sealed the game.Played under the haunting dome of Tropicana Field, it felt like the quintessential Rays game. They refused to strike out, put the ball into the field of play, and put pressure on the Yankees to make plays, pressure the Yankees wilted under. This strategy doesn’t work all the time (remember, the Yankees both scored more and allowed fewer runs than the Rays this year), but when it does work, it can make the opponent look silly for trying to win any other way. If you squint, the Yankees really have won their way; in a 1-1 ballgame with the bases loaded in the fifth, Cody Bellinger hit a ball 103 mph off the bat at a 27 degree angle, a combination that produced a home run 57 percent of the time in the regular season:But Bellinger’s particular batted ball was to the deepest part of the park, and it settled into Jonny DeLuca’s glove a foot in front of the wall. If Bellinger could have pulled the ball just a little more, if he swung just barely harder, the Yankees could have been the team that surged ahead 5-1. Instead, Bellinger was left with nothing but a loud out, and the Yankees imploded in the next half-inning.Outside of the continued brilliance of Ben Rice, there’s just not much to hang your hat on here. The Rays executed about as well as they possibly could given the circumstances, and the Yankees couldn’t have played much worse. New York returns to the Bronx deservedly trailing 2-0 in the ALDS for the second season in a row, having been undressed on the road by a division rival each time. As dire as it seems now, the season isn’t over; we all remember what happened in Game 3 last year. But we also remember what happened in Game 4, which underscores how deep of a hole the Yankees find themselves in yet again. They’ll need to find a minor miracle and pull out three in a row against Tampa Bay, or else find themselves trudging once more into the cold winter.On the site today, Jeremy names the Yankees player of the game from Game 2, which had only one possible choice. Also, Madison recaps the White Sox/Guardians matchup from yesterday, Jonathan profiles Ruben Sierra for our Yankee Birthday series, and Peter delivers his At-bat of the Week, which features George Lombard Jr.

The Cycplus AS2 electric bike pump has dipped under £50 for the first time in this Amazon Prime Day deal
item.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
item.content:encoded: Amazon Prime Big Deal Days are here, and there are 48 hours of cycling bargains to be had from October 6th to 7th.There are plenty of cycling deals, some better than others, but one of the best I've seen so far is on the Cycplus AS2 Electric Pump, which has dropped from £59.99 to under £50 for the first time – its best-ever price.As deal-hunting expert and a long-time fan of the Cycplus range, the AS2 is easily one of the best electric pumps I've used. It even earned a spot in our buying guide as our top recommendation for hassle-free, non-manual inflation.Below you'll find all the details, and I'd advise moving quickly, because when Prime Day ends at midnight on the 7th October, so will these deals.The Cycplus AS2 offers game-changing electric pumping. Weighing just 97 grams, it's small enough to fit in a jersey pocket or saddle bag and eliminates the effort of manual mini-pumps. Capable of reaching up to 100 PSI and recharging via fast USB-C, it offers a fast, painless solution for fixing roadside punctures without adding unnecessary bulk to your ride setup.View DealThe AS2 Pro takes electric tyre inflation a step further by adding a digital LED display for real-time pressure monitoring and customizable PSI target presets. Weighing 120 grams, it remains exceptionally compact while offering a higher maximum pressure of 120 PSI and a larger battery for faster inflation times. It also has an auto-shutoff function once the desired pressure is reached.View DealThe AS2 Pro's headline feature is the large LED screen, with a pressure gauge function, allowing for easy reading of preset pressure values and real-time readings. For US Prime Day, it's available at one of its lowest-ever prices.View DealThe main difference between the AS2 and the AS2 Pro lies in control and power: while the original Cycplus AS2 is an ultra-lightweight (97g) single-button inflator with no screen, the AS2 Pro adds a digital LED display that lets you set precise target pressures with a handy auto-shutoff. So if you require precise pressure, the Pro model is the way to go.The Pro version also boosts maximum output from 100 to 120 PSI and inflates faster thanks to a larger battery.There are a few drawbacks to be aware of when using any electric pumps. They can get quite hot when using them, so you need to be aware when using inner tubes with plastic valves, because they can melt. If you still use inner tubes, the AS2 range comes with a heat-protective extension hose to alleviate this, and a heat reducing protective sleeve, but be aware they don't get that hot when held in your hand.They have to be charged too, so remember to do that before heading out.In my opinion, the positives outweigh those negatives, and the convenience of use, precise pressure levels (especially with the Pro model and its LED screen), and the lack of effort when it's required are all box-tickers for me.

item.title: Want to go Strava-free? The Cateye Padrone is a brilliantly simple bike computer, and it's under £40 for Amazon Prime Day
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: The best bike computers can do almost everything and are now packed with technology to track your ride data, offer maps for navigation, and even provide advanced features such as health monitoring, custom training plans and additional safety features. Of course, there's nothing wrong with any of those things, but what about cyclists who want a low-tech option that skips the bells and whistles? That's where the Cateye Padrone comes in, and it takes a very different approach to many modern bike computers. There's no GPS, no smartphone connectivity and no Strava integration - just an easy-to-read screen showing the basics, including speed, distance and ride time. In our review, Immy Sykes gave it 4 out of 5 stars, praising its simplicity and the distraction-free riding experience it offers.To access Amazon Prime deals, you'll need a Prime membership. You can sign up for a and cancel anytime before the $14.99 per month fee kicks in.Cateye has been making bike computers since the early 1980s, so it knows a thing or two about what works. The Padrone is a great example, offering a simple but well-designed cycling computer.At 67.5 x 43.0 x 14.5mm, it’s small enough to be discreet, but not so small that you’re having to squint from your position in the saddle. The easy-to-read screen remains clear even in bright sunlight.The device detects movement and automatically starts and stops, so you don't even need to remember to switch it on. It's then easy to glance down and check your current or average speed, without getting drawn into a sea of data. Sometimes, that's all you really need.If you’re a weight weenie, you’re in for a treat too. At only 31.6g, the Padrone is one of the lightest bike computers you’re likely to find. As for battery life, the simplicity continues. The Padrone is powered by a small battery that lasts approximately a year with one hour of use per day, so there are no charging cables or extra accessories to worry about - or inevitably lose.If you ride regularly in unfamiliar places, are heavily invested in training metrics or want seamless integration across multiple platforms, then you may want to look elsewhere. But if you want simple metrics for a distraction-free ride, great battery life and a reliable interface, all in a lightweight and affordable package, the Cateye Padrone is a great pick.This UK-only deal saves you 31%, bringing the price down to just over £38. item.title: Yankees news: Youth Movement in the Bronx
item.author: John Griffin
item.content:encoded: MLB.com: Yesterday afternoon, Major League Baseball announced the finalists for this year’s Hank Aaron Award. Recognizing the two best offensive performances (one in each league), the award is conferred through a fan vote and a panel consisting of journalists and former players. Yankees first baseman/designated hitter Ben Rice finds himself as one of this year’s finalists, hoping to make it the three straight season (and fourth in five years) that a Yankees slugger takes home the award (Aaron Judge won it in 2022, 2024, and 2025). Other nominees include Baltimore’s Pete Alonso, Houston’s Yordan Alvarez (the likely favorite), and Kansas City’s Bobby Witt Jr.The Athletic | Clark Gilmore: Clarke Gilmore, a current member of the Savannah Bananas and a former teammate of Ben Rice at Dartmouth, penned a guest article for ’s Peak newsletter, a series focusing on the mental side of sports. As you might have guessed based on the nature of the series, Gilmore spoke not about Rice’s physical prowess, but on his “consistency” that dated back to his college days — and could be seen not only on the diamond, but in much more mundane things, such as Mario Kart in the dorms.FanGraphs | Matt Martell: Turning our attention from one Massachusetts boy to another, Cam Schlittler came out with a completely unexpected strategy against the Red Sox in Game 1 of the ALWC: the typically fastball-dominant youngster threw 32 curveballs — a whopping 27.4 percent of the time (during the regular season, he threw it just 9.8 percent of the time). The start was the culmination of a year-long process in which the Cy Young favorite working to turn his curveball into a veritable weapon, one that can can make him a dangerous pitcher not just now, but going forward.

item.title: Lowest ever prices on Wahoo Bolt and Roam for Amazon Prime Day - Huge discounts on two of our favourite bike computers!
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days are now live, with some serious discounts on bike computers, including 36% off Wahoo's Elemnt Bolt V3 and 26% off the Elemnt Roam V3. The two computers sit alongside each other in Wahoo's range, with the Elemnt Bolt offering a compact, no-nonsense package and the Elemnt Roam adding a larger screen, touchscreen and longer battery life for riders who want more navigation-focused functionality. We've been impressed with both, with each earning 4.5 out of 5 stars in our reviews.The Wahoo range has consistently impressed our test team, with several models holding coveted places amongst the best bike computers on the market. The Elemnt Roam V3 is no exception, securing a spot in our best bike computers guide.Despite its small footprint, the Elemnt Bolt V3 offers all the key training, riding and navigation features most cyclists are likely to need, packed into a compact, aerodynamic package. It was already really good value in the context of bike computers nowadays – and now, it's even better value.View DealThe Bolt has been a mainstay of Wahoo's bike computer range for years, offering plenty of functionality in a compact, no-nonsense package. The third-generation Bolt V3 builds on that formula with a better screen, longer battery life and more storage, while keeping the compact design we've always liked.At RRP, it's one of the cheapest computers on the market to offer this level of functionality, and now with more than $100 off for US readers, it's even more appealing.Despite its size, the Elemnt Bolt packs in a huge amount of functionality. It covers all the essentials, from tracking distance, speed and ride time to providing navigation when you need to find your way. It's also straightforward to set up and use, making it a great option for newer cyclists who want to start tracking their rides and training, while its low weight - a feathery 84.8g - and compact design will appeal to more performance-focused riders too.This is also the lowest price the Bolt has ever been on Amazon, beating the March 2026 price of $297.49 comprehensively. The Elemnt Boltdoes miss out on a touchscreen, so if you want something a little bigger and more navigation-focused, the Elemnt Roam V3 is the one for you.While many of the features are shared with the Elemnt Bolt, the larger screen and touchscreen make the Roam particularly useful for navigation. It’s a more capable option for riders who want a bike computer that can handle longer adventures while remaining straightforward to use.The navigation screen itself is fantastic, and this is about as large as you really need. The display is vivid and easy to follow, while the comprehensive base maps make it difficult to miss a turn.A big part of what earned the Roam V3 its place in our best overall guide is its ease of use. This is one of the easiest bike computers to live with, with everything designed to be as straightforward as possible. For what the Roam V3 offers, I think it’s priced more or less bang on the money, and US readers can now pick one up with a big saving during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.Like the Bolt, this is as cheap as the Roam has ever been on Amazon, which bottomed out at £357.94 in December of last year. In his review of the Roam V3, Senior Tech Writer Will Jones said it was "likely the best Wahoo head unit you can buy right now". Meanwhile in his review of the Bolt V3, he described it as a "cracking little bike computer that offers more or less everything its bigger sibling does at a much more justifiable price".Both are strong options, but they cater to slightly different riders. The Bolt is the smaller, more affordable choice, while the Roam offers a larger touchscreen, longer battery life and more navigation-focused features. We'll be keeping a close eye on Amazon Prime Big Deal Days and bringing you more of the best cycling deals.

item.title: Aleix Espargaro back to MotoGP in latest Honda shuffle
item.author: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded: Honda test rider Aleix Espargaro will return to MotoGP action at this weekend’s Indonesian Grand Prix, replacing fellow test rider Taka Nakagami as stand-in for the unwell Joan Mir.Espargaro has been drafted in because Nakagami crashed out on his very first lap of the weekend last time out at Motegi and broke his collarbone. Espargaro’s return to action doesn’t just mark his first time racing since last year’s season finale at Valencia, but it's one of the few times he'll ride a MotoGP machine since a private test crash at Sepang in April left the three-time race winner with a career-threatening shattered back.He fell during a private outing alongside Nakagami at the Malaysian circuit earlier this year, breaking four vertebrae and needing to be medically evacuated back to Spain before requiring multiple surgeries to stabilise the fractures. “It is always a great honour to join the factory Honda team in MotoGP,” said Espargaro in a team statement. "I want to say thank you to them for trusting me to ride while Joan and Taka recover. “After the crash at the start of the year and my injury, I have not had as much time on the bike as I would like, and we travel to Mandalika with realistic expectations as I’ve had only a small number of laps and it’s a really physical track before we even speak about the weather. “Let’s understand how we can best help the team and Honda this weekend and focus on that.”The former Aprilia racer spent the opening months of the year focused on Honda’s current RC213V machine, splitting duties with Nakagami while the Japanese rider concentrated on their new 2027-spec 850cc Pirelli-mounted machine until he was forced to take on double duty as test rider for both machines.That saw him joining the factory team at the Austrian Grand Prix to replace Mir before heading to Japan as a scheduled wildcard on the current 1000cc machine, with Somkiat Chantra deputising for Mir before returning to his regular Honda World Superbike duties this weekend.However, with Nakagami now out of action thanks to the broken collarbone he sustained at Motegi one week ago during that wildcard outing with Honda’s test team, it may well mean that Espargaro has been briefed to take it easy this weekend at Mandalika. Another crash would leave Honda in dire straits in the final few months of development for the new bike before handing it over to their 2027 race team.There has been no further update from Honda on Mir’s condition, with the team reporting before the Japanese Grand Prix that he continued to recuperate at home under the care of his medical team as he undergoes "a series of tests" with "the goal to uncover the root cause of a variety of symptoms the Honda HRC Castrol rider has been suffering from for several months".

item.title: Amazon Prime Day Bike Deals Live: All the best discounts as soon as we unearth them
item.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
item.content:encoded: The nights are drawing in and the spectre of Black Friday is already looming large on the horizon, but you needn't wait for that slightly overwhelming extravaganza of capitalism to pick up some sweet deals, as Amazon is handily having another Prime Day event, or '', to follow official vocab guidelines. It is running from Tuesday 6th October (today) to Wednesday 7th October (tomorrow) with cutoffs at midnight, to make you feel like Cinderella. Along with a crack team of seasoned deal hunters, I'll be dropping anything saucy on this page as we find it. There are already good deals unearthed on wahoo bike computers to kick things off, and the cream of the crop is just below this intro to save you precious effort. Prime Day sales in particular always throw up a lot of useless rubbish, if we are being perfectly honest with you. We're not here to flog any old tat that would be destined for landfill, but rather to unearth the diamonds in the rough; stuff we've used ourselves, rate highly, or know is decent through our trusted contacts. You will naturally need a Prime membership to take advantage of any discounts, but you can just do a and be sneaky about it; I won't tell Uncle Jeff.USA: Prime Day bike dealsThink is a brilliant light for the money, despite not being the most up-to-date model. It has a huge 200-hour runtime and a smart motion sensor. Plus it's very bright, you won't be dissapointed on this light.View DealThe current price for the Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is an all-time low. A perfect chance to get your indoor setup for winter sorted. This is a fantastic indoor trainer.View DealThis is the cheapest Wahoo's smallest computer has been all year, so it's a great time to nab one if you need an upgrade. It doesn't have the touchscreen of the Roam below, but it's lighter and basically has all the same features. last year at full price, so it's even more of a good buy now. The easy navigation and classically friction-free user interface of Wahoo tech were standout features, plus all the usual training aids you'd expect from a device used in the WorldTour. View DealNot as big a discount in percentage terms as the Bolt, but the Roam, but in cash terms they're both about the same. Unless you want the weight savings, and as long as you can afford it, then I'd get the Roam; it's what I use as my own bike computer, and I also gave it 4.5 stars in my review. What sets it apart for me, along with all the things that make the Bolt great, is the brilliant mapping. It's so clear, and the integration of things like Strava Live Segments is excellent for those who like to have a hit out on random lanes at any given moment. View DealChoosing a first bike is hard, but our Associate Editor has just taken delivery of a one of these himself for his son, so it has our seal of approval. Big tyres and self-centring steering help kids as as young as 9 months get started zooming about the place causing havoc. View DealIf you want a larger bike computer but don't want to fork out for a Wahoo or a Garmin, then this could be the one for you. My colleague Tom gave it a 4.5-star review very recently, and rates it as rivalling the established players for performance. More than that, it's stayed on his bike after the review was completed, which is always a good sign. It's got a good app, a big screen with responsive touchscreen capabilities, and for the size, it's relatively lightweight. It could well upset the Garmin/Wahoo apple cart in time. View DealIt's OK; I won't tell anyone if you do a bit of running on the side. I do, on occasion, and a running watch helps a lot to pace yourself as much as anything. The Forerunner 165 is about all you need for regular jogging, and eschews all of the Garmin bells and whistles in terms of internal multisport features to keep the cost down.View DealThe Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is also discounted by around £100. It's a good-quality trainer that comes with handy dropout adaptors, and the Cog and Click system means you can run it with nearly any bike you want to. View DealHere's the UK version for the SEEMEE 300 deal. For £35.52, this is a really excellent little light that does everything well; it's one of our favourite cycling products of the last few years.View DealAs someone who uses Qobuz rather than Spotify so I can listen to my music in HD, they've been a revelation, and the battery life and comfort aren't half bad, too. I can't go back to other headphones now, which is a bit annoying. View DealAs neat light sets go, this is hard to beat. The Hori mounts under your computer, or into your computer mount itself, allowing your computer to sit atop it; plus it has a remote so you can keep your hands on the bars. Pair that with the small but punchy SEEMEE 50 at the back, and you have an effective be-seen setup that'll cover you for short excursions out of the city limits. View DealOK it's not Amazon, but this deal is too big to not include. I described the Gabba R as 'close to faultless for its intended use' when I reviewed it back in 2024, and if you want to ride hard in the rain, it's really hard to beat, especially with such a massive discount. The aesthetics won't be for everyone, but when it's raining, it looks less shiny than it does in the catalogue. View DealHaving recently started a YouTube channel for Cyclingnews, I can tell you a 360 cam is the way to go if you want to do likewise, and while I haven't used the new one from DJI, it's a very trusted brand and it's on an extremely healthy discount. Throw in a few spare batteries so you don't have to stop filming to recharge, and a selfie stick, and you're well on your way to making some sweet, sweet content. View DealPOC helmets are perennially popular here at Cyclingnews, and the latest do-it-all road/gravel option is already on sale, leaving £60 in your pocket. You get the classic POC aesthetics, the latest MIPS Air Node safety features, and a port on the back for mounting a Knog light (sold separately). Go for white for the pro look, or orange for safety, or get a slightly lesser discount on some more jazzy options. View Deal

item.title: While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution | Charlotte Hill
item.author: Charlotte Hill
item.content:encoded: Food businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out thereCharlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation FelixHow often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes about three meals a week, or 156 meals a year.Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector, more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food is wasted each year in the UK for the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to 470,000 tonnes – enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount – and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious.Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation FelixContinue reading...

item.title: The action Mercedes can take over confusing F1 upgrade
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Mercedes is keeping all options on the table, including running a potential back-to-back test with its old package in Singapore, to try to understand why its latest Formula 1 upgrade did not deliver the step forward hoped for.However, rather than unleashing a predicted 0.3-second gain in laptime, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff wondered if it had actually resulted in a step back of up to 0.5 seconds as rival Red Bull took its first victory of the season with Max Verstappen.Mercedes was at a loss to explain why improvements being shown on the data in terms of extra downforce were not manifesting themselves in the laptimes.And it was particularly perplexed about why the gains it had made in high-speed corners had come at the cost of low-speed performance, and had appeared to impact its straightline speed as well.The key answer Mercedes needs from what happened in Malaysia is how much of its performance deficit was down to the new package and how much of it was down to the unique circumstances of the Sepang event - with high temperatures and a rough track surface.As world championship leader Kimi Antonelli said: "That's the question we need to answer because we don't really know if it made us go faster or worse."It's fair to say, this season that whenever we went on really old Tarmacs, we've struggled."For example, in Zandvoort, McLaren was much quicker than us, especially on the older Tarmac. So, I think maybe it's just a question that the Tarmac is just very old and that for the tyres it's very, very hard, and maybe we just struggle on this kind of Tarmac."While the track surface could explain its problems in slow corners, it would not have impacted its top speed.But deputy team principal Bradley Lord thought this was probably mostly related to extra downforce added to the car having resulted in more drag."That's probably one of the lesser question marks," he said. "We know that adding downforce that brings with it drag, and the calculation is that what you gain in the corners will outweigh what you lose down the straights."We've seen what we're expecting there, we're seeing the benefit in the high-speed corners and the medium-speed - and the drivers say they can feel it as well. "But there's no doubt that we've struggled in certain corners all weekend, particularly the slower ones."Lord later said in Mercedes' post-weekend debrief: "The combination potentially of updates, track temperature and track surface caused an interaction, a set of behaviours that meant the car was not in its usual happy state, that the drivers were having to turn the car on the throttle in the slow corners. That was further exacerbating the challenges of tyre temperatures."So that's not an easy thing to unpick. It's a bit of a 3D problem that we need to work through, and then figure out exactly what steps we take going forward to make sure that we've got the base understanding we need to understand that the update is working well and that we're heading in the right direction in our development, not just for this year's car, but for next year as well."Mercedes is set for some intense engineering debriefs over the next few days to try to get to the bottom of what happened in Malaysia, and work out how best to get answers for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.It is understood that the squad is open-minded about how best to tackle the issue and that nothing is off the table right now.One possibility to fast-track an answer about what has happened could be to run the Mercedes cars in different configurations in practice in Singapore so it can gather real-world data about the gains and losses from the new upgrade.If it concludes that the upgrade has not worked, then it is not ruling out rolling back on it long term despite the logistical complications that would cause.Equally, Mercedes could ultimately conclude that the Malaysia showing was a one-off caused by the heat and track surface, and it sticks to pushing on with the new parts on both cars.What Mercedes does for Singapore depends on what conclusions are found early this week. There's also the added complication of Singapore being a sprint event with only one practice session on Friday. Lord said: "There are many things to unpick. We've seen some teams without upgrades take a step forward this weekend."Other upgraded teams have taken a step forward, while [some other] teams that have upgrades have performed less well than we might have expected."We're not the only people with some questions to answer as we leave the weekend. But certainly we've got to unpick what is down to what and understand if that has any implications on how we head into Singapore and the remaining six races after that."

On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. item.title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
item.author: Gaby Hinsliff
item.content:encoded: Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through itThere’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil.And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection, without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool, and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet, an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistContinue reading...

item.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
item.author: Morwenna Ferrier
item.content:encoded: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?Temperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.Continue reading...

item.title: Yankees make a million errors, drop Game 2 of the ALDS to Tampa
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: I hate Tropicana Field. I know many of you do too. If you are not a Yankees fan and are doing what I am also guilty of doing—reading the reactions of salty fans after playoff losses—grab your popcorn. This is the good stuff you’re probably looking for.It blows my mind that baseball games in 2026 are played at places like this. It honestly blows my mind even more that this place was destroyed by an act of God two years ago, was rebuilt despite plans to replace it in the near future, and is being used for big playoff games. The roof is baseball-colored; there is statistical proof that teams other than the Rays struggle defensively here due to a lack of experience; the turf leads to weird hops that cause more errors to be committed against Tampa Bay than any other team in baseball. It’s the strangest home-field advantage in baseball, and one that the Rays ran roughshod over to take advantage of a Yankees team that was just not focused from the jump tonight—and one that, to be clear, absolutely deserved this atrocious loss, even if it was played in the baseball version of Elysian Fields.Alright, enough of my anger-filled soapbox. The Yanks set the tone for this one with three brutal first-inning errors, played shoddy defense the rest of the night, and just got Rays’d. Any opportunity they had to use their speed or slap hitting, they used it. The Yankees were not prepared. Aside from two home runs from Ben Rice and an oh-so-close deep fly out from Cody Bellinger with the bases juiced, the offense was dead again in a 5-2 loss that puts the season on the brink.When you get no-hit for nearly eight innings the game before, you desperately want to get the monkey off your back early the next night. The quality of contact was good in that first inning against Freddy Peralta, with a warning-track fly out from Rice and a scorched Bellinger lineout, but the Yankees went quietly in the first before the utter chaos of the bottom half.On just Cam Schlittler’s second pitch of the game, Yandy Díaz hit a soft Trop chopper to Ryan McMahon, which he promptly booted after misreading the hop. Jonathan Aranda then lined a single up the middle for the one real hit in the inning. Needing a double play, Schlittler got Junior Caminero to spike a ball into the turf that was snared by George Lombard Jr. for a brilliant flip for a forceout. Unfortunately, Jazz Chisholm Jr. decided to throw the ball into the dugout with no chance to turn two, giving the Rays the early lead.The defensive inning from hell continued when a three-pitch strikeout from Liam Hicks was overturned into a catcher’s interference error on Austin Wells. Awarding a batter a base for a check-swing catcher’s interference is dumb, and I will forever believe that. The speedy Chandler Simpson ripped a ball to second for what looked like a tailor-made double play, but an awful throw from Chisholm pulled Lombard off the bag. The rookie shortstop somehow managed to tap the bag after to avoid a fourth error in the inning, and Cam survived the inning from hell with only one run allowed.We got more Trop shenanigans when Spencer Jones hit a ball a mile high off the B-ring in center field, which was caught by Victor Mesa Jr. Objectively, almost every other team drops that ball because of their lack of experience reading fly balls here, but the Rays caught it, naturally. Two more quick outs had Peralta rolling through two.Jonny DeLuca golfed an 0-2 curveball in the dirt for a leadoff double in the second, but was stranded on a trio of groundouts surrounding a two-out walk. The bottom of the order went down quietly as well, giving Peralta a perfect game through three innings just one night after Rasmussen’s brilliance. At this point, I’m not sure the vibes could get much worse.Schlittler continued to grind through the third, allowing singles to Caminero and Simpson, but got out of a jam after a 108.5 mph scorched grounder from DeLuca was fielded cleanly by Lombard to end the threat. Just one batter later, with the Yankees entering their 13th inning of the series with just one hit, Rice allowed everyone on the team and in the fanbase to breathe for a second, smashing a leadoff home run in the fourth to tie the game at one.Bellinger followed with a single, but was stranded by the next three hitters. Schlittler responded to the desperate gasp for a shutdown inning, retiring the Rays in order with help from a surprisingly solid play by Trent Grisham in center field. Peralta seemed to be cruising again after retiring the first two in the fifth, but things got interesting after a bullet double by Austin Wells and a gritty walk by Ryan McMahon. The ever-aggressive Kevin Cash pulled him for Cam Booser, betting on his lefty specialist to neutralize the best hitters on the team.He walked Rice on five pitches to bring up Bellinger with the bases loaded. This was the moment. This was where the Yankees could show who they were. For a brief second, it seemed like they would. The All-Star left fielder absolutely pummeled a bad 0-2 fastball to deep center field. 102.9 mph, 405 feet. In 12 ballparks, it’s a grand slam. In some others, it’s off the wall. Unfortunately, as has happened all too many times in the postseason in the Judge era, the big hit fell just a few inches short, landing harmlessly in the glove of DeLuca.It’s the type of gut punch that takes the air out of a fan, and maybe it took the air out of the team. It’s not how baseball works, but maybe it is. Schlittler allowed a bullet single (that Jones maybe should’ve caught?) and a bullet double from Caminero to set up second and third with nobody out. Usually, a team’s cleanup and five-hole hitters wouldn’t be conducive to 55 and 65 mph choppers that bounce two feet in front of home plate in RBI opportunities, but these are the Rays. Both runs scored on back-to-back Baltimore chops that the Yankees had no chance of getting an out at the plate on, even if Lombard had defended the latter cleanly. That gave the Rays a 3-1 lead.The frustration didn’t end there. After Brent Headrick entered and struck out Mesa, we got another Trop chop grounder to Lombard. Due to the bounce the ball took and the speed of DeLuca, he had to rush the throw, which forced a long stretch from Luis García Jr. If the play was made cleanly, DeLuca would’ve been out by an eyelash, which tells you how perfect they had to be, but García couldn’t squeeze the throw, and everyone was safe. Another error. One batter later, Richie Palacios hit a two-run single to effectively ice this one, making it 5-1 Rays. We then hit a weird point in the game. Ian Seymour came in for the Rays as a lefty bulk reliever, but Aaron Boone elected to keep his righties in the dugout. As a fan who was resigned to the outcome after the Palacios single, it seems like nothing, but damn, that’s pretty rough of your manager to be so apathetic in this spot. The lineup had no pulse against him in some rough matchups.Playing out the string, John Schreiber tossed a scoreless sixth, Ryan Weathers and Paul Blackburn combined for the seventh, and Blackburn and David Bednar combined for the ninth. For the offense, all they had left was another home run for Rice, who continues to have a postseason to remember while his teammates give him no help, like 2018 LeBron. Bryan Baker got the save in the ninth, 1-2-3, to solidify Game 2 for the Rays. If the Yankees want to win this series and get to the ALCS, they must win three straight against a team they’ve struggled against all year and win a game at Tropicana Field on Saturday after going 2-7 there to start this season. We’re essentially right back where we were a year ago with the Yankees down 0-2 and leaving Toronto. Bleak, I know.There will be baseball played on Wednesday. After that, it’s up to the Yankees to decide. Game 3 will be at Yankee Stadium at 8 pm EDT. It’s Max Fried (pending the birth of his child) against a pitcher to be determined, but it will likely be Nick Martinez.
